paras: The attempted lynching of James T. Quarles and Henry Williams took place at Nampa, Idaho, shortly after midnight on May 25, 1903, when a crowd broke into the jail to seize the two Black men from Boise after Quarles was accused of shooting a Nampa officer at a baseball game. Officers kept the mob from the prisoners, and Governor Morrison took them to Boise by special train. The attack ran in wire reports as far as Atlanta and Maine, while Idaho papers outside Boise called it exaggerated; Quarles was later convicted of assault with a deadly weapon and fined $150.

On Sunday, May 24, 1903, the Boise baseball team played at Nampa, and fights between Nampa and Boise men followed the game. By the Walla Walla Evening Statesman's account, Quarles protested when a Nampa man hit a Boise boy and "was knocked down by several men and badly beaten"; Officer John N. Grogan fired his revolver, and Quarles, on the ground, fired twice, hitting Grogan in the leg and shoulder. Quarles ran but was caught, and Williams, who had taken his part, was arrested with him. Early dispatches feared Grogan's wound would prove fatal, and threats of lynching were heard that evening.

According to a telephone message from Nampa at 12:15 a.m., a crowd of fifteen men then tried to lynch the two prisoners. They obtained the jailer's keys, entered the jail, and took the cell keys by force from Chief of Police Lillard. A later Boise dispatch said the men reached the first steel cage but not the second, then "determined to shoot the prisoners" and were seeking a light when Lillard, Mayor Sutherland and a few others arrived.

The first wire said a dozen special officers drove the crowd out after "a lively scrimmage." Governor Morrison and the sheriff came on a special train, the mob followed them to the train without resistance, and the prisoners were in the Boise county jail by 4 a.m.

The governor and the Canyon County prosecuting attorney said the mob's ringleaders would be prosecuted, but no report of charges against any member of the mob appears in the coverage. Quarles was later reported held for a preliminary examination and then freed on $2,800 bond. At Caldwell on December 10 a jury found him guilty of assault with a deadly weapon and asked the judge for the lightest possible punishment; Judge Stewart fined him $150.

The short wire ran on May 25 under "Idaho Mob Tried to Lynch Negro" in the Atlanta Constitution and "Try to Lynch Negroes" in the Birmingham Age-Herald, and the next day in the Daily Kennebec Journal of Augusta, Maine. Western papers printed fuller dispatches: the Salt Lake Herald headed its story "Negro Escaped Mob," and the Evening Statesman called Quarles a San Juan Hill veteran with "a good record and reputation." These reports named the prisoners as "colored" or "negroes" but gave no race for the mob.

Idaho papers outside Boise played the attack down, and the Silver City Nugget called the affair "a real good show but scarcely worthy of the scare heads in the Boise papers." The Caldwell Tribune blamed Boise "toughs" and the two "Boise negroes," said the mob spirit faded before the crowd reached the jail, and called the Boise papers' coverage "disgusting." A Salem, Oregon, paper joked about the episode and reported the policeman killed, and December reports of the verdict recalled that Quarles had "barely escaped lynching."

Accounts of the shooting differed. The Weiser Signal said Grogan himself knocked the Black man down and fired twice before Quarles returned fire, while a Nampa dispatch in the Teton Peak said Quarles first struck Grogan with a cane. The Caldwell Tribune said Quarles drew his gun on a telephone man and shot at Grogan after a contractor released his wrist.
The Caldwell Tribune also reduced the jail attack to "a half-hearted little demonstration on the jail" by a few men, against the wire reports of a mob inside the jail.

bases: A crowd entered the Nampa jail to lynch two Black prisoners held over the shooting of an officer and was driven off by officers before anyone was harmed, an attempted lynching (A1, A5, A10).

A crowd of about fifteen acted without authority to kill two prisoners over the shooting of an officer, but officers kept them from the prisoners and no one was killed (A1, A5); it was an attempted lynching.

A Boise telephone report, a later Boise dispatch, the Weiser Signal and the Caldwell Tribune independently report a crowd moving on the jail to lynch the prisoners (A1, A5, A10, A23), though the Caldwell Tribune reduces it to a 'half-hearted' demonstration.

accounts.gist: The mob reached the first steel cage, decided to shoot the prisoners and sought a light, but Lillard, Sutherland and a few others held it off until the governor and sheriff arrived.

accounts.label: Weiser Signal
accounts.gist: The Black man was knocked down by Grogan and beaten before shooting back; a mob took keys to get him out for lynching and was stopped by a posse.

accounts.label: Nampa dispatch (Teton Peak)
accounts.gist: Quarles struck Grogan with a cane, Grogan fired in the air, Quarles fired twice; lynching threats were made but the crowd quieted.

accounts.label: Caldwell Tribune (Canyon County)
accounts.gist: Boise toughs and two 'Boise negroes' caused the trouble; Quarles shot Grogan after a contractor released his wrist; the crowd's mob spirit faded before the jail and only a few made a half-hearted demonstration.

framing.detail: Southern and eastern papers ran the short wire under 'Idaho Mob Tried to Lynch Negro' and 'Try to Lynch Negroes,' identifying the prisoners by race and not the mob.
The Salt Lake Herald's 'Negro Escaped Mob' reported the mob's plan to shoot the prisoners and the official vow to prosecute ringleaders.
The Evening Statesman's 'Riot at Nampa Game' headed Quarles as a 'San Juan Hill Negro Veteran' who 'Puts Bullet in Officer' but reported he was beaten first and had a good record.
The Caldwell Tribune blamed Boise 'toughs' and 'Boise negroes,' treated the lynching impulse as natural ('It took—it always takes'), minimized the jail attack and praised Nampa's respect for law.
The Silver City Nugget and Salem Daily Journal treated the affair as comic material about Idaho baseball.
